summary: Defines the X.509 certificate profile used to show who holds the right to use Internet number resources. It is the normative description of certificate and revocation list syntax in the RPKI. It was later updated by RFC 7318, RFC 8209 and RFC 9829.

eli5.summary: These are digital ID cards saying that someone holds a block of internet addresses or network numbers. This defines exactly what goes on the card.

questions: what is in an rpki certificate
what is an rpki resource certificate
subtitle: The strict recipe for X.509 certificates that prove who holds which IP address blocks and AS numbers.

tldr.problem: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure needs certificates that say an issuer has granted a holder the right to use specific IP addresses and AS numbers, and every implementation must read them the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The profile narrows ordinary PKIX certificates and CRLs to a fixed set of required fields and extensions, adds resource extensions that list the numbers held, and defines how relying parties validate a certification path, including checking that each certificate's resources fit inside its issuer's.
tldr.outcome: It is the normative definition of certificate and CRL syntax in the RPKI. It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 7318, RFC 8209 and RFC 9829.

today: RFC 6487 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7318, RFC 8209 and RFC 9829, and has not been obsoleted. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: A Certificate Profile for Internet Number Resources
sections.content:
This document defines a profile of X.509 certificates for certifying Internet Number Resources (INRs), meaning IP addresses and Autonomous System (AS) numbers. Such certificates are called resource certificates. A resource certificate conforms to the PKIX profile in RFC 5280 plus the extra constraints here, and it attests that the issuer has granted the subject a right of use for a listed set of addresses and AS numbers.

The profile is an integral part of the Certificate Policy for the RPKI (RFC 6484), and it is the normative specification of certificate and CRL syntax in the RPKI. Besides certificates and CRLs, it also profiles certificate requests and the relying party's path validation procedure.

The central rule is strict: the fields the profile lists MUST be present, and any extension not explicitly mentioned MUST be absent. The same holds for CRLs. Number registries issue the certificates, so the RPKI lines up with how addresses and AS numbers are allocated: when a registry allocates a resource to an entity, a certificate can describe that allocation and bind the subject's key to it.
sections.eli5: Think of a card that says 'this person may use these street numbers'. The rulebook says exactly what must be on the card and that nothing else may be added.

sections.title: Resources and End-Entity Certificates
sections.content:
Resources are described with the extensions from RFC 3779. This profile requires every resource certificate to contain the IP Address Delegation extension, the AS Identifier Delegation extension, or both, and both MUST be marked critical. Resources use the sorted canonical format with maximal spanning ranges and prefix masks, except where the inherit construct says the certificate takes its resources from its issuer.

When validating, a relying party MUST check that the issuer's resources encompass the subject's: the issuer's resources may be the same as, or a strict superset of, the subject's.

The profile also covers end-entity (EE) certificates. Their main job is to verify signed objects about the use of the resources, such as Route Origin Authorizations and manifests. The EE certificate is embedded in a CMS signed-data structure, and its private key signs a single signed object. Because of this one-to-one link, revoking the certificate effectively revokes the object. An EE certificate that signs a sequence of objects, each overwriting the last at the same publication point (for example a sequence of manifests), is a "sequential use" certificate. One that validates only a single instance is a "one-time-use" certificate.
sections.eli5: Each card lists which numbers its holder may use, and a card can only list numbers that its issuer also holds. A special small card signs exactly one document, so tearing up the card cancels that document.

sections.title: What Goes in a Resource Certificate
sections.content:
Unless a field is marked OPTIONAL, it MUST be present, and fields not listed MUST NOT appear. The version MUST be 3 (the field value is 2), and relying parties need not process version 1 or 2 certificates. The serial number is a positive integer unique per issuing CA. Signature and public key algorithms come from RFC 6485.

Issuer and subject names are X.501 distinguished names. A name MUST contain one CommonName, encoded as a PrintableString, and MAY contain one serialNumber. Names are not meant to describe identity and are not required to be globally unique, though CAs are advised to generate names that make collisions unlikely. The issuer picks the subject name, not the subject, and it SHOULD use a different subject name if the subject's key pair changes.

On validity, a CA may issue a certificate whose period extends beyond its own, and a notBefore or notAfter may fall outside the superior certificate's period. Relying parties SHOULD NOT infer validity at any time other than the present.

Extensions follow strict rules. Subject Key Identifier MUST appear and is the 160-bit SHA-1 hash of the subject public key. Authority Key Identifier MUST appear except in self-signed certificates. Key Usage is critical: CA certificates set only keyCertSign and CRLSign, and EE certificates set only digitalSignature. Extended Key Usage MUST NOT appear in CA certificates or in EE certificates used to verify RPKI objects. CRL Distribution Points and Authority Information Access MUST be present except in self-signed certificates and point, preferably by an rsync:// URI, to the issuer's CRL and the issuer's certificate. Subject Information Access points to what the subject publishes: for a CA, the repository directory (id-ad-caRepository) and its manifest (id-ad-rpkiManifest); for an EE certificate, the signed object (id-ad-signedObject). Certificate Policies is critical and holds exactly one policy.
sections.eli5: The card has a fixed list of boxes to fill in, like name, serial number, dates, a pointer to the issuer, and the list of numbers. Extra boxes are forbidden, and CA cards and signing cards have slightly different rules.

sections.title: Revocation Lists and Certificate Requests
sections.content:
Each CA MUST issue a version 2 CRL, and relying parties are not required to process version 1. Indirect and Delta CRLs MUST NOT be used, and each CRL covers all certificates issued by that CA. If several CRLs exist, the one with the highest CRL Number supersedes the others. Every CRL MUST include the Authority Key Identifier and CRL Number extensions and no other extensions. Each revoked entry carries only the serial number and the revocation date.

A request for a certificate MAY use PKCS#10 or the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF). A CA MUST support PKCS#10 and MAY support CRMF. The profile defines no certificate response: for a CA certificate the CA places it in the repository, and none is defined for EE requests. With the exception of the public key and the Subject Information Access request, the CA may alter any requested field. The subject name in a request SHOULD be empty so the CA generates a unique one. The Subject Information Access extension MUST be present in a request, and if the CA cannot honor it, the CA MUST reject the request.
sections.eli5: When a card is cancelled, its serial number goes on a short public list. To get a card, you send in your public key and the issuer decides most of the rest.

sections.title: How Relying Parties Validate a Certificate
sections.content:
Validation refines the generic process in RFC 5280. The key idea is the resource comparison. A range is more specific than another if the other includes all of it and is larger; two ranges are equal if they describe the same set; and a set X encompasses a set Y if every range in Y is more specific than or equal to a range in X. Along a certification path, the resources in each certificate must encompass those in the next one, and the trust anchor's resources must encompass those of the first certificate.

The path must start with a certificate issued by a trust anchor, and the subject of each certificate must be the issuer of the next. Each certificate must satisfy these checks:

  • Its signature verifies with the issuer's public key.
  • The current time lies within its validity period.
  • It has every field that MUST be present and none that MUST NOT be.
  • It is not revoked: its serial number is not on the issuer's current CRL, that CRL is valid, and the key verifying the CRL is the same key that verifies the certificate.
  • Its resources are encompassed by the previous certificate's.

The checks may run in any order. Certificates and CRLs may come from a local cache synchronized with the distributed repositories. Because malformed or looping paths could be used for denial of service, an implementation MAY halt validation with a failure if the path length exceeds a locally configured limit.
sections.eli5: To trust a card, you walk up the chain of issuers to one you already trust. At every step you check the signature, the dates, that the card was not cancelled, and that its numbers fit inside the issuer's numbers.

sections.title: Changing the Profile Later
sections.content:
Because relying parties must reject anything that does not conform, any future change to the profile is not backward compatible. The RFC explains why this is manageable in the RPKI: every CA is also essentially a relying party, many small holders use managed CA services from Regional Internet Registries, and RPKI relying party software comes from a limited number of sources. The critical flag on extensions is not a general solution.

If the profile changes, a new document will update this RFC and the Certificate Policy will define a new policy OID and a timeline of three phases. By the end of phase 1 all CAs MUST be able to issue under the new profile if asked. In phase 2, CAs MUST issue under the new profile alongside the old format, with the two kinds of certificate identical except for the policy OID and new items, and relying parties may use either. In phase 3, all relying parties MUST be able to process the new format and CAs issue only under it. At the end, support for the old format is removed.
sections.eli5: If the card design ever changes, everyone first learns to make the new card, then both kinds are handed out for a while, and finally only the new kind remains.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5280 and RFC 3779 apply to resource certificates, and those of RFC 2986 and RFC 4211 apply to requests.

A resource certificate PKI cannot by itself resolve ambiguity when two or more valid certificates encompass the same resource. If issuance follows the allocation and assignment records, then a certificate is only as good as the databases it reflects.

The profile requires that the key signing a certificate is the same key that signs the CRL able to revoke it. This is tighter than normal X.509. The RFC warns that a validation implementation using separate paths for a certificate and its CRL carries risk: if subject names collide because CAs did not use enough entropy in names, an out-of-profile relying party could conclude a valid certificate was revoked.
sections.eli5: A card is only as trustworthy as the records behind it. The same key must sign a card and its cancel list, so no one can slip in a fake cancel notice.
